passage: Thursday Lakshmi asked me "Is this right, Sir?" eleven times during one maths lesson. I counted. Her eyes filled up when I said, "You already know it is." She hardly speaks at break, just stands near the classroom door. I nearly said "Stop worrying" again. It didn't help last week. Instead, at the end of the day I sat beside her and asked quietly, "What's the scariest part of maths for you?" She whispered, "Getting it wrong and Amma being sad." I called her mother tonight. We agreed on a plan: Lakshmi gets two check-in cards a lesson; after those, she has a go on her own. At home they'll try the same. She's a kind, careful child. I want her to feel safe, not rescued every minute. - Akash

qa.q: How many times did Lakshmi ask 'Is this right, Sir?' in one lesson?
How does Akash feel about Lakshmi when he writes that he wants her to feel safe?
qa.a: He feels caring and concerned for her, and wants her to feel safe rather than rescued every minute, which is why he stopped saying 'Stop worrying'.

qa.q: What plan did Akash agree on with Lakshmi's mother?
qa.a: Lakshmi gets two check-in cards a lesson and then has a go on her own, with the same idea at home.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi feel about having two check-in cards a lesson?
qa.a: Lakshmi may feel nervous at first about trying alone, but safer knowing she still has two chances to check.

grounding: A teacher notices a child seeking constant reassurance and tearful, uses gentle questions and a calm tone, and makes a plan with the family that neither dismisses nor feeds the worry.

passage: Since his father left for work in the city, eight-year-old Manoj had grown very quiet. At the village well, at the shop, at night, he asked Jaya the same thing: "Will Papa come back? What if he doesn't?" At first she said, "Of course he will, don't ask again." He asked twice as often. Then one evening, while shelling peas on the step, she asked softly, "What makes you think he won't?" Manoj's lip wobbled. "Raju's father went and never came." Jaya put the peas down. She didn't laugh or scold. She called his father on the phone that night, and his teacher the next day. Together they made a calendar on the kitchen wall with call days ticked in red and the day Papa comes home circled. Each morning Manoj ticked one box himself.

qa.q: What did Jaya and Manoj make on the kitchen wall?
qa.a: A calendar with call days ticked in red and the day Papa comes home circled.

qa.q: Why was Manoj so worried his father wouldn't come back?
qa.a: Raju's father went to work away and never came back, so Manoj feared the same.

qa.q: Which change in Jaya's approach helped?
qa.a: She stopped brushing off his question and asked gently what made him think so, then made a plan with his father and teacher.

qa.q: What might it be like for Manoj to tick a box on the calendar himself each morning?
qa.a: It likely makes him feel calmer and more in control, because he can see the calls and the day Papa comes home getting closer.

grounding: An adult notices a child who is quiet and constantly seeks reassurance, asks gentle questions, and makes a plan with the family and teacher.
